                            between-group differences in peak Qcon or peak Hecc , in accordance with our results. The
                            contrasting results on Hecc between the present study and the study of O’Connor et al. [29]
                            could be explained by the different criteria used to separate groups (low (<65) and high
                            (>85) ACL-RSI scores for cases and controls in the study by O’Connor et al. [29] compared
                            to <81.4% and >81.4% in the present study). Having some individuals from different groups
                            but with very close ACL-RSI scores in the present study could have biassed the results
                            towards a lack of between-group differences. Other differences between studies are the
                            significantly larger sample size in O’Connor [29]’s study (n = 452) and their cut-off at nine
                            months post-surgery, compared to the range of longitudinal time frames examined within
                            this study. It can be hypothesised that athlete perceptions within O’Connor’s [29] study
                            are more of a reflection of their rehabilitation process. In contrast, for our participants who
                            have returned to sport and, thus, benefit from greater sporting exposures, ACL-RSI scores
                            illustrate the development of psychological barriers for athletes in the pursuit of a return to
                            PILOS, which is a novel element of the current study. Finally, our data analysis was based
                            on a linear regression, in contrast to correlations in the study of O’Connor et al. [29], which
                            may explain the lack of association between some parameters and the ACL-RSI scores.
                                  A novel finding of the present study is the significantly lower Qcon40 and Qcon30 in
                            cases compared to controls (differences of 21% and 23%, respectively, at these angles). The
                            role of the quadriceps at these shallow flexion angles is significant in relation to the number
                            of ACLI that occur within them [21]. Previous studies have shown that individuals with
                            weaker quadriceps have altered sagittal plane kinematics during landing and subsequently
                            incur higher GRF upon a stiff-legged landing [19]. Similar to our comments on RTD, this
                            process may result in a perception of instability during sport participation that could be
                            reflected in the ACL-RSI scores. During rehabilitation, restoration of joint ROM is targeted
                            during the early phases [46], yet little consideration is noted regarding muscular strength,
                            specifically functionally important ranges (near full knee extension) in which non-contact
                            ACLI occur (Hammond [24]). Our findings on angle-specific torque, together with the
                            absence of significant differences between groups in peak torque, highlight the importance
                            for physiotherapists to address strength deficits across the full range of motion and consider
                            sport-specific mechanics (i.e., movements such as landing or side cutting, where the knee
                            might not be very flexed, supporting stipulations made by Hammond [24], who similarly
                            reported strength deficits between specific angles, where >90% LSI was achieved during
                            peak torque assessments). The importance of the capacity to produce high torque when
                            the knee is close to full extension has also been highlighted in a study on fatigue in female
                            footballers, showing that Hecc :Qcon was significantly reduced after a simulated match only
                            between 0 and 10◦ from full knee extension [34]. This highlights the reduced capacity
                            of the hamstring to stabilise the knee joint close to extension in a fatigued state, where
                            ACLI occurs, and highlights the importance of addressing residual strength deficits at these
                            angles during rehabilitation.
                                  The limb symmetry index has been cited as a risk factor for lower limb injuries in
                            previous literature [47], although there are contrasting results in the literature [48]. Our
                            findings did not identify it as a major determinant of psychological readiness to RTS,
                            suggesting that it might not be sensitive enough to affect athletes’ perceptions during
                            exercise. However, we found that LSI for RTD100 in the quadriceps at both testing velocities
                            was greater in cases than controls. This highlights one more time that power rather than
                            strength could be an important factor that could play a role in athletes’ decisions to RTS.
                                  The main limitations of the present study are the lack of control over our participants’
                            rehabilitation and subsequent sport experience. Indeed, we could not capture the exercise
                            types, volume, and frequency of rehabilitation sessions or past/current sport participation
                            due to the long time lapse between the start of rehabilitation and testing for some of our
                            participants. In addition, we chose to focus on psychological parameters as our main
                            outcome and explore the role of strength and power variables as potential determinants
                            of this. However, an argument can be made that constructs such as fear and confidence
                            may instead impact physiological parameters through the avoidance of high-intensity

                                   rehabilitation required in order to efficiently address them. Finally, our sample size was
                                   small, in particular in comparison with the study by O’Connor et al. [29], which could
                                   limit the interpretation of our findings; however, this is counteracted by the fact that we
                                   observed relatively large effect sizes. We also recruited athletes from specific sports, which
                                   might limit the application of our findings to other sports. The main strengths of our
                                   study are the wide and novel range of outcome variables considered (in particular, RTD
                                   and angle-specific torque data) and the controlled laboratory conditions in which data
                                   was collected.

                                   5. Conclusions
                                         In conclusion, our findings showed that one of the main determinants of psychological
                                   readiness to RTS following ACLR was the RTD of the quadriceps and hamstrings. In
                                   addition, compared to controls, cases showed significantly lower angle-specific quadriceps
                                   torque close to extension and lower quadriceps RTD, but no difference in peak torque values.
                                   The importance of muscular strength across all angles of function was also identified, with
                                   quadriceps strength of particular importance at angles of functional relevance between 20◦
                                   and 40◦ from full extension. These findings highlight the importance for physiotherapists
                                   to address muscular deficits across their full range (by choosing some exercises with the
                                   knee joint positioned near full extension) and develop power and explosiveness in addition
                                   to strength in rehabilitation. Future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to further
                                   investigate the relationship between strength and power and psychological factors playing
                                   a role in RTS.

{
 "id": "Q42",
 "sourceFile": "The role of virtual reality in the management of football injuries.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text, 'The Role of Virtual Reality in the Management of Football Injuries' (Medicina 2024), matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
  "Brain Health & Psychology"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training",
  "Rehabilitation",
  "Performance"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Soccer"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Mixed / Unspecified",
  "Male Athletes",
  "Female Athletes",
  "Healthy Athletes",
  "Injured Athletes"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "The authors describe this as a narrative review, but it used a described search of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science with two reviewers screening and extracting data. It summarizes virtual reality studies in football across prevention (cognition, biomechanics, heading), post-injury care (low back pain, concussion education, kinesiophobia), with summary tables of small, mostly single-session laboratory studies (samples of 2 to 60 participants). The authors report that VR can reproduce sport-specific movements, showed gains in passing decisions and heading goals, reduced pain and kinesiophobia in some studies, and that evidence is limited by a lack of standardized protocols and randomized trials.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review has no pooled effect estimates, uses a single author-chosen search, and relies on small studies, several with no control group. The evidence is mostly from laboratory or short-term studies, so it cannot show that VR reduces injury incidence or speeds return to play.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the favourable VR findings as proof that VR lowers injury risk or speeds rehabilitation, when the included studies are small, short and mostly not randomized.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Demeco A, Salerno A, Gusai M, Vignali B, Gramigna V, Palumbo A, et al. The Role of Virtual Reality in the Management of Football Injuries. Medicina. 2024;60:1000.",
  "doi": "10.3390/medicina60061000",
  "abstract": "The review summarizes virtual reality (VR) approaches for football injuries, covering prevention (biomechanical risk assessment, perceptual-cognitive training, heading), rehabilitation (low back pain, return to sport, kinesiophobia) and concussion education. It is framed around the high injury burden in football and the need for individualized prevention and rehabilitation.",
  "tldr": "VR can recreate sport-specific movements and has shown early benefits for decision-making, heading, low back pain and fear of movement in small studies. Its effect on injury rates and return to play has not been established.",
  "methods": "Narrative review of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science from inception to 10 February (year not stated), using lesion, rupture or injury terms combined with virtual, mixed or extended reality terms and soccer or football. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts and extracted data; a third resolved disagreements. Reference lists were also searched.",
  "findings": "The review's tables list 14 studies, mostly single-session laboratory work with 2 to 60 participants. Reported results include VR training improving passing decisions and visual search in young players (Fortes et al., 2021), VR-trained players scoring more headed goals than controls over 10 days (Marshall et al., 2023), and VR reducing pain and kinesiophobia in players with chronic low back pain (Nambi et al.). A single-session VR concussion education study in children (Sullivan et al., 2024) found no significant change in attitudes toward reporting or reporting intentions.",
  "limitations": "The authors state that there is no standardized VR protocol and no randomized controlled trial of VR exercise efficacy, and that the reliability of VR movement analysis in sport is unproven. Most included studies are small, short and single-session, and the review does not pool results.",
  "practicalImplications": "Sports medicine and performance staff may consider VR as a supplement for perceptual-cognitive or biomechanical training and for low back pain or fear-of-movement work, where the evidence is preliminary. Its use for injury prevention or return-to-play decisions is not supported by the evidence reviewed.",
  "athleteDev": "VR is a possible training aid for decision-making and heading skills in footballers, based on small studies with short follow-up. Coaches should not expect large or proven performance gains from it.",
  "rtp": "VR may support post-injury rehabilitation for low back pain and kinesiophobia, and may be used to simulate sport-specific tasks during the late rehabilitation phase. The review does not establish VR as a return-to-play test, and clearance decisions should not rely on it."
 }
}

16	
17	
18	                                           Abstract: Injuries represent a serious concern for football players, with a significant loss in terms of
19	                                           sport participation and long periods of rehabilitation. According to the 2019/20 UEFA Élite Club
20	                                           Injury Report, the average incidence of injuries during training is 2.8 per 1000 h of training, with

74	                                Muscle strains, ligament sprains and contusions were the most common, with thigh
75	                          strain representing 17% of all injuries, and posterior thigh strains more common than
76	                          anterior ones. Furthermore, adductor pain/strain, ankle sprain and medial collateral
77	                          ligament (MCL) injuries are relatively frequent [3].
78	                                Muscle injuries constitute 31% of all injuries and cause 27% of total injury absences. In
79	                          total, 92% of all muscle injuries affect the four major lower limb muscle groups: hamstrings
80	                          (37%), adductors (23%), quadriceps (19%), and calf muscles (13%). Moreover, quadriceps
81	                          strains (60%) affect mostly the dominant leg (preferred kicking leg) and the incidence
82	                          is six times higher during a match compared with training [3,4]. Muscle injuries have
83	                          been classified into non-structural and structural injuries [5]: non-structural lesions, which
84	                          comprise 70% of muscle injuries in football, do not lead to theanatomical interruption of
85	                          muscle fibers. In these cases, the athlete usually reports tenderness, heaviness, or a feeling
86	                          of stiffness in the affected muscle, which increases with the continuation of sports activity
87	                          and sometimes occurs at rest. Upon palpatory examination, stiffer muscle bundles can be
88	                          found within the interested muscle. Moreover, re-injury represents a serious concern by
89	                          causing more prolonged absences, and players with a history of previous injuries tend to
90	                          have a re-injury risk that is 4 to 7 times greater [3].
91	                                What predisposes the athlete to a relapse is both risk factors related to the changes that
92	                          occurred after the first injury (muscle hypotrophy, scar tissue, neuromuscular changes), as
93	                          well as inadequate treatments (aggressive or incomplete rehabilitation, underestimation of
94	                          primary injury, prolonged immobilization).
95	                                In addition to muscle injuries, one of the most common injuries concerns ligaments;
96	                          in particular, anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture has a serious impact on footballers’
97	                          careers. The ACL provides stability to the knee joint, preventing the anterior displacement
98	                          of the tibia relative to the femur. A complete rupture is a cause of knee instability and can
99	                          lead to long-term knee conditions, such as meniscosis, osteoarthritis, and a high rate of new
100	                          lesions in the graft or contralateral knee [6,7]. A study based on 78 teams participating in
101	                          UEFA competitions between 2001 and 2015 recorded 157 cruciate ligament injuries, of which
102	                          140 were total and 17 were partial ruptures, including six relapses and two contralateral
103	                          injuries; the average frequency of cruciate ligament injuries is 0.066 per 1000 h. The full
104	                          injury had a significantly higher average frequency than partial rupture (0.059 vs. 0.007 per
105	                          1000 h), and the frequency of injuries during matches was greater than 20 times compared
106	                          to workout [8]. ACL injuries usually occur through traumatic mechanisms without contact,
107	                          mainly during high-velocity movements, such as a quick change of direction, a sudden
108	                          stop, or a landing after a jump [8].
109	                                One of the most discussed risk factors for injuries is fatigue, defined not as energy
110	                          exhaustion during a game, but an effect of fatigue accumulation over a period of time,
111	                          presumably due to a dense schedule of matches [9]. In addition, several intrinsic and
112	                          extrinsic factors pose a higher risk of injuries, such as intrinsic biomechanical factors,
113	                          hormonal, anatomical and neuromuscular risk factors, as well as limited hip and ankle
114	                          mobility, which could predispose the knee to higher loads [10]. There are also some gender-
115	                          related risk factors, which show that female populations have a particular predisposition
116	                          (e.g., for ACL injuries), presumably due to the role of estrogen receptors and progesterone
117	                          in female populations [11].
118	                                Injuries are therefore a serious problem not only for players but also for clubs as, on
119	                          the one hand, the chances of the whole team performing optimally are limited; on the other
120	                          hand, they also represent a cost to society (the average cost of a professional player injured
121	                          for a month is about EUR 500.000) [8].

123	                          1.2. Injury Prevention
124	                               Injury prevention is essential for reducing the long-term consequences and minimizing
125	                          the impact on the sports season. It is recommended that an approach be based on the

130	                          individual athlete’s lifestyle, not solely on managing risk factors. Several injury prevention
131	                          programs like FIFA 11+ and PEP have been developed in recent years [12,13].
132	                                The focus is the perception of the fatigue of athletes, which can be avoided by main-
133	                          taining proper hydration, nutrition, and following individualized training protocols with
134	                          appropriate loads. Moreover, muscle weakness and the difference in strength between
135	                          agonist and antagonist muscles increase the risk of injury by 4 to 5 times. Therefore, it is
136	                          crucial to objectively and quantitatively evaluate athletes periodically [14,15].
137	                                Prevention exercise programs with a comprehensive approach play a key role in
138	                          reducing the incidence of injury. It has been shown that specific prevention programs such
139	                          as Sportsmetrics and the Prevent Injury and Enhance Performance Program reduce the risk
140	                          of injury and positively impact performances [16].
141	                                Eccentric exercise training is the method most used for preventive purposes because it
142	                          causes a muscle adaptation that significantly improves the stiffness of the muscle–tendon
143	                          unit. Moreover, proprioceptive training has also shown interesting results; it must be
144	                          preceded by adequate heating, in monopodalic and bipodalic alternating support, on stable
145	                          and unstable surfaces with dynamic exercises and adequate technical material [17]. Finally,
146	                          selective core muscle training can also improve the neuromuscular control of the lower
147	                          limbs, and working on balance has been proven effective in reducing the rate of anterior
148	                          cruciate ligament injuries [10].
149	
150	                          1.3. Rehabilitation
151	                                In case of injury, rehabilitation is of vital importance, with specific treatments based
152	                          on the type and site of injury, and the grade of lesion. In most injuries, the treatment is
153	                          conservative, with reduced workloads, active recovery with hydrokinesitherapy and the
154	                          application of physical therapies [7]. The type of rehabilitation and therapeutic proposals
155	                          must respect the principle of specificity, progression, and individualization. It is essential to
156	                          consider pain as an indicative factor for the load capacity, with a progressive load needed
157	                          to allow complete and optimal tissue regeneration [18,19]. When returning to play, it is
158	                          important to apply the correct progression of sport-specific training, which is enabled
159	                          by the sanitary staff’s constant monitoring and correct communication with the technical
160	                          staff [6].
161	                                In case of surgical treatment, pre-operative rehabilitation is fundamental, with the aim
162	                          to control pain and inflammation through cryotherapy, compression and anti-inflammatory
163	                          drugs, the recovery of ROM through active and passive mobilizations, and the strengthen-
164	                          ing of quadriceps and hamstrings through exercises in the closed kinetic chain, possibly by
165	                          using electrical stimulation and proprioceptive education [20].
166	
167	                          1.4. Virtual Reality
168	                                Alongside the classic rehabilitation techniques and various protocols for injury man-
169	                          agement, we have observed the swift advancement of new technologies such as virtual
170	                          reality (VR). VR can be defined as “a medium comprising interactive computer simulations
171	                          that detect the position and movements of the subject, giving the feeling of being mentally
172	                          immersed in the virtual world”.
173	                                Through various tools, including headsets, gloves, shoes and joypads, the experience
174	                          is enriched, and the three-dimensional environment appears real [21].
175	                                It is possible to distinguish three types of virtual reality, each with its specific charac-
176	                          teristics [21,22]:
177	                          •    Immersive VR creates a three-dimensional room in which the subject is immersed with
178	                               no reference to the real world.
179	                          •    Non-immersive VR is generated through computers and consoles, allowing the visual-
180	                               ization of 2D virtual objects in the real context.
181	                          •    Mixed reality combines immersive and non-immersive virtual reality: the technology
182	                               is generated by head-mounted displays that overlap with the real-world 3D virtual
183	                               objects (holograms), allowing interaction with them.

188	                                In the medical field, VR has shown interesting results in numerous applications,
189	                          mainly in motor and cognitive rehabilitation and the therapy of psychiatric disorders, such
190	                          as anxiety and depression [23]. Currently, VR-based rehabilitation is used particularly in
191	                          the neurological field for balance disorders and impairment of the upper limbs following
192	                          stroke [22].
193	                                This technology has become increasingly popular in recent years, as it provides a
194	                          secure and controlled environment for performing various actions. In addition, using VR
195	                          constitutes a motivating and engaging rehabilitation approach for the patient, with the
196	                          possibility to customize the treatment based on the patient’s needs [9].
197	                                Among the critical issues that emerge from the use of VR in healthcare are the costs of
198	                          equipment, the need for technical expertise, and cybersickness, defined as the nausea and
199	                          headaches caused by the prolonged use of smartphones, tablets and headsets [24].
200	                                In sport, VR can be seen as an assistive technology that provides specific support
201	                          for training through the simulation of game dynamics and data analysis. However, the
202	                          applications of VR vary, and include the improvement of teamwork and reductions in the
203	                          risk of injury throughout a personalized training program for a single player based on the
204	                          data collected, helping them to improve their weaknesses and reach their potential [24,25].
205	                                In addition, athletes who undergo a rehabilitation program involving VR describe the
206	                          experience as rewarding, pleasant and motivating, increasing their compliance [26].
207	                                VR’s interactive and immersive nature can aid in conducting training sessions and
208	                          enable accurate statistical analysis. Athletes can practice on a simulated field using headsets
209	                          and head-mounted displays while collecting and analyzing crucial data in real time, e.g.,
210	                          heart rate and blood pressure, to evaluate the effectiveness of their training [24].
211	                                To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has summarized the role of VR in
212	                          the management of football injuries. Thus, the aim of this narrative review is to provide
213	                          a broad overview of the currently available VR approaches used to reduce the incidence
214	                          of injuries and improve the rehabilitation outcome, promoting a personalized strategy for
215	                          the multidisciplinary management of footballers. In details, this review analyzes the role
216	                          of VR for preventive purposes through a study of the biomechanics of athletic gestures
217	                          in a realistic environment and the reduction in concussions; the rehabilitative purposes,
218	                          improvements in pain symptoms, return to sport, and kinesiophobia are also analyzed.

250	                          3. VR in Injury Prevention
251	                               VR has immense potential in the field of preventive medicine, as it allows for the
252	                          creation of personalized, immersive exercises that can effectively prevent injury. By simu-
253	                          lating various scenarios that focus on specific athletic gestures, training programs become
254	                          more engaging, safer, and better tailored to the sport. Additionally, VR serves as a valuable
255	                          research tool for assessing risk factors in conditions that closely resemble those experienced
256	                          in the field. By recreating virtual environments and protected game scenarios that mirror
257	                          real-life situations, it is possible to collect and analyze biomechanical and kinematic data
258	                          close to the match dynamics. See Table 2 for further details.
259	
260	                          3.1. Cognitive Ability and Speed of Execution
261	                                Football is constantly evolving, athleticism is increasingly important, and the speed of
262	                          the game is much faster than in the past; this leads to increased cognitive engagement, and
263	                          quick and accurate decisions must be made based on retrieving and processing information
264	                          from a dynamic environment. Therefore, football players must improve their cognitive–
265	                          perceptual skills to avoid the adverse effects of mental fatigue during training and matches.
266	                          Superior perceptual–cognitive motor skills promote the formation and development of
267	                          motor skills, and high levels of perceptual–cognitive spatiotemporal ability can effectively
268	                          improve performance [27,28]. In football, the player must move the neck, head, and eyes
269	                          to perceive the position of teammates and opponents in the environment and then make
270	                          the most appropriate decision based on the current situation. The processes of anticipation
271	                          and decision-making are the key skills of a football player. Namely, anticipation is the
272	                          ability to recognize the outcome of other athletes’ movements before they are executed;
273	                          decision-making is defined as the ability of the human brain to extract meaningful con-
274	                          textual information from the visual scene, and visual exploration behavior is part of the
275	                          mechanisms behind decision-making. Anticipation and decision-making are important
276	                          requirements for players because of the variable and high-velocity environment [29]. The
277	                          game is intense, the situation on the field is fluid, and players must react quickly and
278	                          accurately depending on the situation [30].
279	                                In this regard, VR could allow video stimulation training to improve the perceptual-
280	                          cognitive abilities of players, creating a virtual world with multiple sensory experiences,
281	                          e.g., changing the number of opponents or teammates and the game situation. In this way,
282	                          it is possible to improve the choice of passage, the speed that is used, and the fixation
283	                          characteristics of the most skilled footballers. Moreover, improving their scanning behavior
284	                          could be especially useful for central midfielders. This would allow them to scan more,
285	                          and a higher frequency is associated with a higher probability of completion [31,32]. The
286	                          transferred skills resulting from VR perceptual–cognitive training could be proportional
287	                          based on the degree of similarity between the training modality and the targeted skill.
288	                          Moreover, the results of a study in the literature showed that VR is superior to other forms
289	                          of training based on 2D video stimulation since it provides more immersive and engaging
290	                          information, optimizes task representation, and effectively improves cognitive–perceptual
291	                          skills [24,27]. However, despite efforts to create environments that are as realistic as possible,
292	                          discrepancies with real life remain inevitable.
293	                                In performance analysis, superior performance is readily apparent on observation,
294	                          while the perceptual–cognitive mechanisms that contribute to the expert advantage are
295	                          less evident; therefore, the ability to create experimental tasks and conditions that allow
296	                          expertise to emerge is a critical factor in players’ selection, and can be defined into specific
297	                          parameters of sports performance [33]. The literature has identified the most prevalent out-
298	                          come measures concerning perceptual–cognitive differences between expert and nonexpert
299	                          athletes [34], including response accuracy, response time, and eye movement features. In
300	                          this scenario, VR can give consistent support in order to distinguish participants based on

322	                          3.2. Psychological Aspect
323	                                Stress and competitive anxiety are two aspects that have received considerable atten-
324	                          tion in the world of sport. Stress occurs when there is an imbalance between the physical
325	                          and mental demands placed on the athlete and the ability to respond in such conditions;
326	                          specifically, psychological stress is the relationship between the person and the environment
327	                          that the person perceives as straining or exceeding his/her resources and endangering their
328	                          well-being [38]. One factor that contributes to psychological stress is competitive anxiety,
329	                          namely the response to a sports-related stressful situation that results in a series of cognitive
330	                          appraisals and behavioral responses. When it becomes too high, the athlete may become
331	                          excessively excited, exceeding their mental ability to process stimuli, resulting in increased
332	                          stress and decreased performance. Competitive anxiety is divided into cognitive anxiety
333	                          (negative thoughts and concerns) and somatic anxiety (physiological signs of nervousness
334	                          and tension) [39]. Therefore, athletes must modulate psychological stress and anxiety
335	                          by developing or discovering positive coping mechanisms for optimal performance and
336	                          well-being. Inadequate coping mechanisms indicate poor adaptability to stress. A negative
337	                          response to stress and anxiety impairs motor coordination, reduces flexibility, increases
338	                          cognitive and somatic anxiety, and shifts attention to narrow the field of vision. The litera-
339	                          ture has extensively analyzed the relationship between sports gesture anxiety; it has been
340	                          found that an increase in anxiety is associated with the deterioration of sports performance.
341	                          It was seen, in fact, that the precision of penalties is inversely proportional to the state of
342	                          seniority; in addition, players’ speed and swing in table tennis worsened with an increase in
343	                          anxiety [40,41]. Athletes’ rising psychological stress and anxiety levels have prompted the
344	                          implementation of several interventions. These interventions include awareness, relaxation
345	                          imagery, deep breathing and muscle relaxation [42]. With the increasing use of technology,
346	                          technological devices have started to be used in the treatment of anxiety. An immersive
347	                          visual experience can result in better results in reducing anxiety compared to traditional
348	                          relaxation techniques. In this context, VR has already been used in both non-sport and
349	                          sport contexts for the treatment of anxiety, with excellent results in terms of relaxation,
350	                          allowing better coping mechanisms to be developed in the professional context [42–44].
351	                                Furthermore, the ability to recreate customized game scenarios, complete with dis-
352	                          tracting factors like stadium noise and opponents, can be a valuable tool in psychological
353	                          training, especially in youth teams. Recent studies have shown that the presence or absence
354	                          of spectators in a football stadium can significantly impact the psychological state, behavior
355	                          and performance of players and football teams [31,45].
356	                                In the contemporary sports landscape, mental coaches have become integral to both
357	                          individual and team sports. This is due to increasing pressure on athletes and the recogni-
358	                          tion that the mental aspect should be trained on par with the physical component. In this

367	                          3.3. Biomechanics Evaluation and Neuromuscular Training
368	                                At the forefront of sports medicine, the novel application of VR technology is revo-
369	                          lutionizing the way we analyze in-game performance data. By immersing athletes into
370	                          meticulously crafted virtual environments, researchers can simulate realistic scenarios,
371	                          enabling them to analyze the athlete’s movements and identify potential risks factors. VR
372	                          technology can be a valuable tool for detecting biomechanical issues specific to certain
373	                          gestures that pose a risk of injury for athletes. The main advantage of this technology is
374	                          its ability to provide a contextualized view of gestures within a particular sports environ-
375	                          ment. For example, in contact sports like football, numerous variables impact the athlete’s
376	                          kinematics and biomechanics, such as the need to avoid or counter an opponent. VR can
377	                          be helpful when athletes need to analyze the angles of their hip, knee, and ankle joints to
378	                          evade opponents, such as when an opposing player is running toward them [25,46].
379	                                For example, it is possible to assess differences in the biomechanics of athletes during
380	                          sport-specific activities, such as jumping and landing, actions commonly executed in a
381	                          football game. In this case, the physician can analyze biomechanics in a VR laboratory
382	                          highlighting, e.g., the differences between a standard vertical drop jump and a VR jump to
383	                          head a ball in a football-specific corner kick scenario [25]. In a study by Di Cesare et al. [25],
384	                          authors showed different values in the two conditions analyzed. In the VR scenario, they
385	                          registered a reduction in hip and ankle flexion in the sagittal plane and a reduction in hip
386	                          and ankle excursion at the peak knee flexion, compatible with a more stiff and possibly
387	                          dangerous landing [47]. This could pave the way for a deeper understanding of game
388	                          biomechanics and related risk factors.
389	                                Moreover, this technology allows athletes to rewatch and examine their movements
390	                          during the session for a patient’s self-correction. The advantage of this diagnostic–
391	                          preventative–monitoring tool is the ability to perform the same exercise several times
392	                          under the same conditions, providing new insights [46].
393	                                Furthermore, it is possible to create an augmented neuromuscular training (aNMT)
394	                          program to enhance proprioception and neuromuscular control. Namely, aNMT aims
395	                          to reduce injuries utilizing biofeedback, giving the participants visual stimuli while they
396	                          execute movements [48]. In the late rehabilitation phase, VR represents a tool to test
397	                          the transferability of the training in the context of sports games, monitoring the athlete’s
398	                          movements performed in a safe environment.
399	                                In one study by Kiefer et al. [49], it was possible to recreate a real side-cutting defensive
400	                          action performed against a non-player character (NPC) within a VR laboratory in which
401	                          athletes could perform exercises as if they were in a football field.
402	                                The visualized virtual environment was simulated using Unity 3d PRO, and partic-
403	                          ipants viewed the environment through a custom-built wireless HMD to allow them a
404	                          greater degree of freedom. In the proposed scenario, the athlete had his back to the goal
405	                          in a football field. At the sound of a whistle, the defensive action began against the NPC,
406	                          advancing toward the goal. The athlete had to run toward the NPC and counter his action
407	                          as it quickly changed direction. This created unexpected lateral cutting actions, which
408	                          varied according to the virtual player’s movements [49].
409	                                In another study by Grooms et al., the athletes underwent specialized training that
410	                          relied on a visual stimulus biofeedback. The purpose of this training was to identify
411	                          and address mechanisms that could potentially lead to injury [50]. Specifically, during
412	                          closed-chain exercise (e.g., squat, single-leg Romanian deadlift, tuck jumps), a rectangle
413	                          that represented the perfect biomechanics associated with the performance of that exercise
414	                          was displayed on a screen, and each time the system detected biomechanics that pose a
415	                          risk to ACL damage, the rectangle started deforming, thereby inducing self-correction in
416	                          the participant. At the end of the training period, changes in lower motor cortex activity

426	                                           increased risk of neurodegenerative pathologies in athletes. While further studies are

428	                                           reduce the frequency of heading drills during training [51].
429	                                                 Limitations have been established regarding the number of football heading move-
430	                                           ments allowed during training and matches. For example, the Football Association of
431	                                           England suggests that players over fourteen years old should not exceed ten headers dur-
432	                                           ing a once-a-week session. For kids up to the age of eleven, it is recommended that headers
433	                                           are not used at all [52].
434	                                                 Moreover, UEFA introduced “UEFA heading guidelines for youth players”, a series of
435	                                           guidelines intended to better manage heading during training by teaching the correct way
436	                                           to tackle heading drills. However, the most important modifiable factors are the ball size
437	                                           and pressure, neck strengthening, less frequent trainings and education [2]. Nevertheless,
438	                                           this limits the possibility of training players to perform headers, lowering the player’s
439	                                           ability to direct the ball correctly. Marshall et al. [53] discovered that the group of players
440	                                           who were trained in headers using VR experienced a significant increase in the number of
441	                                           goals scored with headed shots compared to those in the control group. Additionally, the
442	                                           VR group reported an increase in perceived confidence and self-efficacy before the second
443	                                           test [53].
444	                                                 VR technology enables the creation of simulated game environments that can be
445	                                           leveraged for training purposes. The use of a point-based system can facilitate the estab-
446	                                           lishment of a ranking system, which can potentially foster healthy competition among
447	                                           participants. Thanks to VR’s ability to simulate diverse and dynamic scenarios, it is possible
448	                                           to populate the environment with NPCs that can engage in offensive or defensive actions,
449	                                           exhibiting both predictable and unanticipated behavior. Balls can be thrown, and their
450	                                           speed, trajectory and acceleration can be manipulated [53]. Moreover, it could be possible
451	                                           to integrate the lack of sensory feedback to the head with tactile stimulations for a more
452	                                           realistic experience [54] However, VR is a promising compromise between the concussion
453	                                           prevention guidelines and performance.

598	                          4. VR in Post Injury Application
599	                               In the post-injury phase, VR has shown interesting results in tailoring exercise plans
600	                          to athletes’ needs, by recreating sport-specific scenarios in a safe environment to bridge the
601	                          gap between rehabilitation and the reathletization, ameliorating the emotional impact of
602	                          the injury and lowering the level of kinesiophobia. See Table 3 for further details.
603	
604	                          4.1. Low Back Pain
605	                               Chronic low back pain (LBP), persisting for more than 3 months, is a prevalent and
606	                          significant issue in football, ranking as the fourth most common disorder with an incidence
607	                          rate of 32–42% per year and with higher incidence in professional athletes [56,57]. The high
608	                          workloads due to training and competitions cause mechanical stress to the musculoskeletal
609	                          system. The diagnosis and treatment of chronic LBP is controversial and there is no clear
610	                          consensus on its optimal management. In addition, most LBP in football players has no
611	                          identifiable etiology. Several causal factors for LBP have been identified, including the
612	                          instability of the trunk muscles, the incoordination of the hip spine during movement, and
613	                          the repetition of excessive lumbar extension and rotation [58]. Trauma to the soft tissues of
614	                          the lumbar region during athletic activity can affect the function of the central muscles and
615	                          lead to muscle imbalance. Changes in central muscle function can lead to a wide range of
616	                          compensatory movements, which can lead to lower back pain. Also, improper activities
617	                          during the training session may be due to abnormal muscle activity, which may further
618	                          aggravate the condition [57]. The movements involved in kicking the ball, placing the
619	                          support foot close to the ball and rotating the trunk at high speed, cause significant stress to
620	                          the lumbar spine and hips. Compared to an instep kick, a lateral kick increases the external
621	                          angle of rotation of the hip, while an outstep kick increases the internal angle of rotation of
622	                          the hip. During a football movement, the presence of LBP shifts the player’s center of mass
623	                          (COM) laterally and rotates the lumbar spine significantly, resulting in additional stress on
624	                          the lumbar spine [58,59].
625	                               In this context, VR can provide valuable support to rehabilitation programs, allowing
626	                          the creation of an exercise plan that aims to improve the functional ability of players
627	                          through neural facilitation, the stimulation of the sensory functions, and motor learning.
628	                          For the upper body, it is possible to plan exercises that improve the core stability and
629	                          balance of abdominal muscles and spinal erectors for proper muscle balance in order to
630	                          prevent and/or treat sports disorders such LBP [31,57,60].
631	                               With the use of a virtual platform in an upright position or sitting position, it is possi-
632	                          ble to perform the movements of torso bending, lateral extension and flexion, selectively
633	                          controlling the speed and difficulty of execution by working on the neuromuscular system
634	                          to facilitate the activity of the motor unit [61]. A HDM or joystick would allow movement
635	                          tracking to be performed, and the difficulty of serious games can be modified according to
636	                          the degree of disability with increasing speeds or a range of motion. The effectiveness of
637	                          VR in rehabilitation programs is supported by scientific evidence. In detail, following a
638	                          treatment program with VR, an improvement in pain, quality of life, and jumping perfor-
639	                          mance that is associated with a reduction in inflammatory biomarkers such as C-reactive
640	                          protein (CRP), tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α), and interleukins has been demonstrated. In
641	                          addition, MRI and ultrasound have shown an increase in the cross-sectional area of the
642	                          multifidus, psoas, and erector muscles of the spine [57,62].
643	
644	                          4.2. Concussion
645	                               Sport-related concussion (SRC) is a type of mild traumatic brain injury that occurs
646	                          when head trauma results in transient neurological impairment, observed commonly both
647	                          in professional and amateur sports [63]. The Consensus Statement from the Berlin 2016
648	                          International Conference on Concussion in Sport has provided a logical flow of clinical
649	                          concussion management and considerations referring to the ‘11 Rs’ of SRC (recognize,
650	                          reduce, remove, refer, re-evaluate, rest, rehabilitate, recover, return-to-learn/return-to-sport,
651	                          reconsider and residual effects). A similar format has been followed for the Amsterdam
652	 Medicina 2024, 60, 1000                                                                                              11 of 17
653	
654	
655	
656	                          2022 Statement, with additional ‘Rs’ including RETIRE, to address issues related to potential
657	                          career-ending decisions, and REFINE, to highlight the need to embrace ongoing strategies
658	                          to advance the field [63].
659	                                In football, though not publicly perceived as the sport classically associated with
660	                          head trauma and concussion, head injuries are mostly caused by head-to-head collisions
661	                          and unanticipated ball contacts, with SRC presenting 22% of football-related injuries.
662	                          Accordingly, 63% of football players have suffered a concussion during their playing
663	                          careers and 82% of athletes who have suffered a concussion have experienced two or more
664	                          concussions throughout their playing careers [64].
665	                                Exposure to acute concussion, repetitive concussions, as well as cumulative “sub-
666	                          concussive” result in athletes having an increased risk of developing long-term neurologic
667	                          impairment, post-concussion syndrome, and structural brain changes detectable on func-
668	                          tional brain imaging [65–68]. Furthermore, having ascertained that concussed athletes
669	                          in American football have increased odds of sustaining an acute lower extremity muscu-
670	                          loskeletal injury after returning to play than their non-concussed teammates, a possible
671	                          connection between subclinical head injury and impairment in proprioception has been
672	                          suggested [69]. Therefore, SRC represents a problem for the health of athletes due to its
673	                          neurological and orthopedic consequences. Data concerning the recognition of the symp-
674	                          toms of SRC suggested that only 19% of patients realize that the symptoms they complain
675	                          of constitute a concussion [64,70,71]. This indicates a lack of player education regarding
676	                          the topic. For this purpose, VR seems to provide a novel tool for instructing athletes to
677	                          recognize the most common symptoms of SRC. Through the use of semi-immersive VR,
678	                          it is possible to educate athletes on the effects of SRC, creating an ideal environment in
679	                          which the player is immersed in the virtual environment as a football athlete playing on
680	                          an outdoor field when a virtual football ball unexpectedly hits them in the head, causing
681	                          them to start experiencing various simulated concussion symptoms (e.g., blurred vision,
682	                          light sensitivity, headache, and nausea) both on the field and after virtually returning
683	                          home. Filmed video clips and scenarios of actual preteen football players reinforce the
684	                          virtual-to-physical relationship by allowing users to see familiar, relatable projections of
685	                          themselves and their environment in the virtual space [72].
686	                                The use of VR technology to teach players, especially adolescents, about concussions
687	                          offers many potential advantages over traditional approaches to concussion education. First,
688	                          VR technology allows athletes to virtually feel and experience SRC in a safe, computer-
689	                          generated environment. These manipulations provide an impactful, experiential, and active
690	                          learning environment, allowing them to enhance their knowledge through experience [72,73].
691	                                In addition, VR can be used to assess the return to play of a football player who has
692	                          undergone an SRC. The need to assess the condition of the athlete after the injury is crucial,
693	                          to ensure the feasibility of returning to the field in concert with the safety and health of the
694	                          athlete themselves. In this regard, the Virtual Reality Football For Concussion Assessment
695	                          has been designed to measure athletes’ performance on immersive, sport-specific tasks to
696	                          improve return-to-play decision-making after a concussion [74].
697	
698	                          4.3. Kinesiophobia
699	                                It is crucial to consider the emotional well-being of athletes in addition to their physical
700	                          recovery when formulating rehabilitation plans. The rehabilitation approach should not
701	                          only focus on restoring the physiological and physical condition, but also address the
702	                          psychological impact on the athletes. A crucial factor that should not be overlooked in the
703	                          rehabilitation of post-injury football players is kinesiophobia. Kinesiophobia is an excessive,
704	                          irrational fear of physical activity or movement due to the increased pain sensitivity caused
705	                          by a painful injury or damage to the body [75]. It may seriously effect recovery, leading to
706	                          increased muscle weakness, increased pain and a decreased level of daily activities [76].
707	                                Some studies have highlighted the moderate prevalence of kinesiophobia in football
708	                          players [76,77]. At present, nonpharmacological therapy is the preferred approach for
709	                          people with chronic pain [78]. Some intervention methods have been studied, such as
710	 Medicina 2024, 60, 1000                                                                                                                            12 of 17
711	
712	
713	
714	                                       cognitive behavioral therapy and graded exposure therapy. However, they reduce the
715	                                       level of kinesiophobia without substantially reducing the pain, which still inevitably
716	                                       affects the rehabilitation process, leading to low compliance and unsatisfactory recovery
717	                                       effects. Exercise, which is recommended as an effective treatment in the context of post-
718	                                       injury rehabilitation [79], may also cause pain to increase dramatically during the sessions,
719	                                       contributing therefore to kinesiophobia. In this scenario, VR has been shown to significantly
720	                                       reduce the level of kinesiophobia, providing rehabilitation training in a novel and attractive
721	                                       way through the creation of a virtual environment that the user can interact with, with
722	                                       a consequently positive impact on the emotional state of the athletes. VR provides the
723	                                       possibility of task-oriented and multisensory feedback training. This facilitates visual,
724	                                       auditory and tactile input, resulting in more accurate and complete motion feedback,
725	                                       exercise capacity development, and exercise compliance improvement. Furthermore, as a
726	                                       complementary therapy, VR has shown more improvements than exercise alone in balance
727	                                       and gait, reducing the fear of falling and promoting the recovery of limb function. In this
728	                                       regard, virtual reality-guided imagery (VRMI) is a great example of how this technology
729	                                       can be implemented to promote psychological readiness and facilitate a smooth transition
730	                                       back to sport [80]. Imagery, specifically, which involves an athlete replicating reality by
731	                                       mentally reviewing an action and picturing visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, and even
732	                                       gustatory cues [81], promotes movement repetition and improves motor abilities in different
733	                                       virtual settings [82]. VRMI based on video-game-based exercises contributes to movement
734	                                       facilitation and functional training in ludic ways, and helps to alleviate psychological
735	                                       distress, including fear of re-injury and pain perception, in first-time ACL restoration
736	                                       patients [83], resulting in more favorable outcomes.
737	                                             Nevertheless, it is important to mention that the inclusion of a high-tech VR tool in
738	                                       psycho-correctional programs, while it has been demonstrated to be useful for overcoming
739	                                       the fear of movement and pain of neuropathic and mixed genesis, remains ineffective in
740	                                       relieving nociceptive pain (i.e., pain where there is no psychological component); therefore,
741	                                       the organic component of the injury should not be neglected [62].
742	                                             One further specification, in conclusion, is about the different natures of VR. Indeed,
743	                                       compared with fully immersive virtual reality, which would provide a better immersive
744	                                       experience and should theoretically achieve better results, non-immersive virtual reality
745	                                       has demonstrated better intervention effects in the context of kinesiophobia [84]. Fully
746	                                       immersive virtual reality requires the use of a head-mounted display as well as a fully
747	                                       occluded peripheral vision, and some participants may experience motion sickness. For
748	                                       this reason, non-immersive virtual reality may be a better option for rehabilitation training,
749	                                       considering its acceptance among the population and its lower cost [85].

836	                                          5. Conclusions
837	                                                Despite its lack of popularity in football, VR has been a valuable tool in rehabilitation
838	                                          for years. The increasing development of technology has inevitably led to the progressive
839	                                          use of innovative tools to improve medical knowledge and positively influence athletic
840	                                          performance.
841	                                                This narrative review highlights the role of VR in rehabilitation and research in foot-
842	                                          ball. Its main advantage includes the possibility of recreating the sport-specific technical
843	                                          gestures as closely as possible. The movement analysis of the athlete and a better under-
844	                                          standing of the biomechanical risk factors could pave the way for an improvement in the
845	                                          treatment protocols used for injury prevention and rehabilitation. Moreover, thanks to
846	                                          the amount of data collected, it is possible to develop a personalized exercise plan based
847	                                          on the athlete’s needs. Additionally, VR represents a valuable tool for investigating and
848	                                          stimulating the cognitive and neuromuscular ability of the footballer, who has to face a
849	                                          high-velocity environment during matches. Indeed, VR environment has the advantages of
850	                                          a standard controlled environment in which the patients can perform exercises subjected to
851	                                          multisensorial stimuli, close to the on-field context. Through virtual reality it is also possible
852	                                          to recreate interacting scenarios, which can educate athletes on how to properly recognize,
853	                                          train and recover from potentially harmful football-related situations, lower back pain, and
854	                                          kinesiophobia in the post-injury phase. Moreover, VR represents one of the few methods
855	                                          that respects the guidelines for concussion prevention, as recommended by the English
856	                                          Football Association, allowing a reduction in concussion-related effects on the brain and
857	                                          the possibility of training players in heading. It could be suggested that the head-mounted
858	                                          displays are improved for a more realistic experience during headings. However, there

                                           two of the most important modifiable risk factors. In this context, prevention and an adequate
                                           rehabilitation protocol are vital in managing injuries, reducing their incidence, and improving
                                           the return to competition. In recent years, technological development has provided new tools in
                                           rehabilitation, and Virtual reality (VR) has shown interesting results in treating neurologic and
                                           orthopedic pathologies. Virtual Reality (VR) technology finds application in the sports industry as a

                                           risk factors associated with anterior cruciate ligament injury. Additionally, VR can be used to train
