196	                                  Athletes’ schedules can negatively impact their sleep and recovery [51,52], and the
197	                           repetitive demanding nature of a competitive season can also test athletes’ physiological
198	                           and psychological capacity, reinforcing the athletes’ need for quality sleep [74–77]. Actigra-
199	                           phy based sleep assessments reveal suboptimal sleep in athletes, i.e., low TST and high
200	                           WASO, causing resultant low sleep efficiency [27,30], which improves following a rest
201	                           day [78]. However, the athletes’ experience of suboptimal sleep remains unclear as sleep
202	                           need varies between individuals; some may report poor sleep while objective measures
203	                           indicate sufficient sleep [32]. Therefore, subjective measures of sleep quality, quantity and
204	                           timing are a valuable addition to objective sleep assessments. Combined subjective markers
205	                           of sleep (e.g., TST, time in bed, sleep efficiency, sleep quality and sleep onset latency) can
206	                           highlight the sleep need and recovery status of athletes and identify areas to be addressed
207	                           in terms of sleep optimisation. Moreover, the use of subjective measures within an athletic
208	                           population allows the assessment of large cohorts of athletes that are difficult to access, i.e.,
209	                           elite athletes.
210	                                  Animal models have demonstrated that nutrients such as glucose, amino acids,
211	                           sodium, ethanol and caffeine, as well as the timing of meals can affect circadian rhythms [79].
212	                           Neurotransmitters such as serotonin, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), orexin, dopamine,
213	                           melanin-concentrating hormone, galanin, noradrenaline and histamine that are involved
214	                           in the sleep–wake cycle [80] are affected by nutrition. In terms of recovery, the adaptive
215	                           response to training is dictated by a number of variables: duration, intensity, frequency
216	                           and type of exercise, in combination with timing, quality and quantity of nutrition both
217	                           pre- and post-exercise [81]. Recovery can be maximised by optimal nutrition practices or
218	                           reduced by suboptimal nutrition practices. Contemporary research has demonstrated the
219	                           pivotal role of both macronutrient and micronutrient availability in regulating skeletal
220	                           muscle adaptations to exercise [81–83]. It is important to characterise the sleep quality
221	                           and quantity of sub-elite and elite athletes and recovery practices. This study aimed to
222	                           investigate: (i) the quality, quantity and timing of sleep among sub-elite and elite athletes;
223	                           (ii) the recovery/stress balance of sub-elite and elite athletes; and (iii) the supplement use
224	                           and alcohol intake of sub-elite and elite athletes. This study also aimed to investigate the
225	                           difference between elite and sub-elite athletes in terms of their subjective sleep, recov-
226	                           ery and nutritional practices. It was hypothesised that the sleep, recovery and nutrition
227	                           practices of elite athletes would be superior to those of sub-elite athletes.

231	                                A sample (n = 338) comprising elite (n = 115; male n = 74 and female n = 41) and
232	                           sub-elite (n = 223; male 129 and female 94) athletes were recruited from both Ireland and
233	                           the United Kingdom (see Table 1). The elite athletes were recruited directly through Sport
234	                           Ireland and the national governing bodies (NGBs) of each sport within Ireland and the
235	                           United Kingdom. The sub-elite athletes were recruited via social media and the researcher’s

243	                           week or (iii) reported a sleep disorder.

260	                            2.2. Procedure
261	                                 All eligible athletes were invited to take part in an online survey. All procedures
262	                            were approved by the research ethics committee of the Faculty of Health and Life Sciences,
263	                            Northumbria University (date of approval 2 July 2019; Submission ID: 17406). After
264	                            reading the participant information sheet, participants were invited to provide informed
265	                            consent and then completed an online survey on Qualtricsxm which consisted of a battery
266	                            of previously validated and reliable widely used questionnaires assessing sleep, recovery
267	                            and nutritional practices. Following completion of the survey, participants received a
268	                            debrief sheet with details of how they could contact the researcher if they wished to receive
269	                            feedback from the survey.

271	                            2.3. Measures
272	                                  In the initial section of the survey, the participants completed demographic data.
273	                            Participants recorded their gender, age, body mass (kg), height (cm), sport, athlete type
274	                            (elite or sub-elite), phase of season (pre-season, competition or off-season), normal training
275	                            time (before 8 a.m., 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and after 5 p.m.) and training/competition duration
276	                            per week (mins).
277	
278	                            2.3.1. EuroQoL (EQ-5D-5L)
279	                                 The EQ-5D-5L is a self-report measure of health status as defined across five dimensions—
280	                            mobility, self-care, activity, pain and depression/anxiety—with one question per dimension.
281	                            Each dimension is scored on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = No problem to 5 = Severe prob-
282	                            lem) [85]. The EQ-5D-5L also includes a visual analogue scale on which respondents are
283	                            instructed to rate their perceived current health state (0–100). The EQ-5D-5L has capacity
284	                            to discriminate between slight, moderate and severe issues within each domain compared
285	                            to previous versions [86].
286	
287	                            2.3.2. Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)
288	                                  The PSQI is a self-report measure of sleep quality [62]. The PSQI consists of 19 items
289	                            grouped into seven component scores (0–3) which are equally weighted. Although overall
290	                            global scores (GPSQI) are calculated by summing the seven components (range 0–21, with
291	                            higher scores indicating poorer sleep quality) the component scores provide subscale
292	                            ratings of: (i) subjective sleep quality, (ii) sleep latency, (iii) TST, (iv) sleep efficiency, (v)
293	                            sleep disturbances, (vi) use of sleep medication and (vii) daytime dysfunction [63]. Global
294	                            scores >5 are generally used to indicate poor sleep quality (63). The PSQI has demonstrated
295	                            a diagnostic sensitivity (89.6%) and specificity (86.5%) in distinguishing between ‘good’ and
296	                            poor’ sleepers [87]. However, more conservative scores of ≥8 have been used in athletes
297	                            to indicate poor sleep, potentially due to the increased sleep needs in this population [55].
298	                            Although the empirical discussion around the PSQI cut-offs for athletes is ongoing [38,55],
299	                            given that athletes often strive for marginal gains in their performance, which can be
300	                            facilitated through optimised sleep, the identification of both ‘poor’ and ‘moderate’ sleep
301	                            quality is warranted [43], hence the standard cut-off (≥5) was employed.
302	 Nutrients 2021, 13, 1330                                                                                            6 of 25
303	
304	
305	
306	                           2.3.3. Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS)
307	                                The ESS is an eight-item self-report measure of general daytime sleepiness [88].
308	                           Respondents report their daytime sleepiness in particular situations on a Likert scale
309	                           (0 = Would never doze to 4 = High chance of dozing). Scores are summed to yield a global
310	                           ESS score (0–24). The EES global score is indicative of daytime sleepiness [89]. Higher
311	                           scores indicate greater sleepiness, scores >10 suggest excessive daytime sleepiness [88].
312	                           In general ESS scores are interpreted in terms of daytime sleepiness as follows: 0–5 low
313	                           normal, 6–10 higher normal, 11–12 mild excessive, 13–15 moderate excessive and 16–24
314	                           severe [65].
315	
316	                           2.3.4. The Recovery Stress Questionnaire for Athletes (RESTQ Sport)
317	                                 The RESTQ-Sport is a 52-item self-report measure of general stress and recovery
318	                           levels of athletes [90]. The RESTQ-Sport consists of seven general stress components
319	                           with two items per scale (general stress, emotional stress, social stress, conflicts/pressure,
320	                           fatigue, a lack of energy, and physical complaints), five general recovery components
321	                           with two items per scale (success, social recovery, physical recovery, general well-being,
322	                           and sleep quality), three sport-specific stress components with four items per scale (dis-
323	                           turbed breaks, burnout/emotional exhaustion, and fitness/injury) and four sport-specific
324	                           recovery components with four items per scale (fitness/being in shape, burnout/personal
325	                           accomplishments, self-efficacy, and self-regulation) [90]. Sub-scale item mean scores can
326	                           be combined to give a total score for each of the four major sub-scales (i.e., general stress,
327	                           general recovery, sport-specific stress and sport-specific recovery). Each item is scored on
328	                           a Likert scale (0 = Never to 6 = Always) based on how often the respondent engaged in
329	                           a specified activity over the previous three days/nights, with a response of 0 indicating
330	                           never having experienced the feeling and 6 indicating always experiencing the associated
331	                           feeling. High scores on stress scales indicate a high level of stress, while high scores on the
332	                           recovery scales indicate a high level of recovery [90].
333	
334	                           2.3.5. Athlete Morningness/Eveningness Questionnaire (AMES)
335	                                The AMES, which is based on the Horne–Östberg morningness/eveningness ques-
336	                           tionnaire [91], is a four-item questionnaire used to classify an athlete’s chronotype in terms
337	                           of self-identification as being a morning or evening type, preferred sleep/wake phase and
338	                           preferred competition and training time [92]. The AMES provides a global score which
339	                           is used to categorise chronotype: extreme evening type (10–12), moderate evening type
340	                           (13–17), mid-range type (18–23), moderate morning type (24–28) and extreme morning
341	                           type (29–31) [55].
342	
343	                           2.3.6. Consensus Sleep Diary—Core (CSD-C)
344	                                 Participants were instructed to complete the CSD-C for two nights (1 ‘training/
345	                           competition’ day and 1 ‘rest’ day). The CSD is a standardised sleep diary developed
346	                           for use in both research and clinical settings [68]. The CSD-C included 8 items, e.g., bed
347	                           time, time it took to fall asleep, number of awakenings, duration of awakenings, time of
348	                           final awakening, time the respondent got out of bed, and a Likert scale self-report rating
349	                           of sleep quality [93]. There was also a comments section where participants could record
350	                           specific comments about each night’s sleep (i.e., 1 training/competition day and 1 rest day).
351	                           The data collected were then used to compute indices of sleep continuity such as total time
352	                           in bed (TIB), total sleep time (TST, sleep onset latency (SOL; time from lights out to N1),
353	                           wakefulness after sleep onset (WASO; amount of time awake after sleep onset), number of
354	                           awakenings (NoA) and sleep efficiency (SE; ratio of TST:TIB) [93].
355

358	                           (name, dose, frequency and reason for use) on both training/competition days and rest

367	                                All data were analysed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS
368	                           Version 25, IBM Corporation) and Jamovi (Version 1.8.16). Frequency distribution and

370	                           ± standard deviation, and/or frequency. The differences between the groups for athlete

Nutrients 2021, 13, 1330. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu13041330                                               https://www.mdpi.com/journal/nutrients
 Nutrients 2021, 13, 1330                                                                                           2 of 25



                           (dehydration, glycogen depletion, muscle damage and mental fatigue), and recovery of
                           muscle function is predominantly a matter of reversing the main causes of fatigue. Sleep
                           deprivation (<7 h) increases circulating stress hormones (e.g., cortisol) [8]; decreases the
                           regeneration of carbohydrate stores (i.e., glycogen) [9]; deregulates appetite and impacts
                           on energy expenditure [10]; increases catabolism and reduces anabolism, impacting the
                           rate of muscle repair (MPS) [11,12]. Therefore, sleep plays a key role in facilitation of
                           post-exercise recovery or the reduction in fatigue and the reversal of the processes that lead
                           to fatigue [13].
                                  Athletes experience stress for various reasons (e.g., training, competition, travel and
                           lifestyle) including periods of both acute and residual fatigue due to heavy training and
                           competition schedules [14]. For example, field-based team sports are characterised by
                           repeated bouts of intermittent activity (sprinting) with short rest periods, representing high
                           physiological stress [15], neuromuscular stress [16,17] and high rates of perceived exertion
                           (i.e., how hard exercise seems) [18]. Further, individual endurance athletes experience
                           fatigue due to prolonged activity, resulting in glycogen depletion, thermal stress and/or
                           dehydration [19]. Relative stress is accumulated when successive bouts of training are com-
                           bined with suboptimal recovery (under-recovery) impacting subsequent performance in
                           training and competition [20]. It has been suggested that decreasing the natural timeframe
                           of the bodies’ regenerative processes via recovery strategies is vital for performance [21].
                           Such recovery strategies can be divided into physiological strategies (e.g., sleep, cold water
                           immersion, cryotherapy, contrast therapy, massage and compression), pharmacological
                           (e.g., non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]) and nutritional (e.g., nutrient tim-
                           ing, composition and supplementation) [22]. However, it must be noted that some research
                           has suggested that interfering with the body’s natural recovery processes, particularly
                           inflammatory responses and OS, could reduce training adaptations [23]. A recent review
                           addressed these concerns in relation to the application of nutritional strategies to reduce
                           muscle damage [24].
                                  Sleep has previously been self-reported as the most important recovery modality
                           utilised by both elite and sub-elite athletes [1,25,26]. Furthermore, it has been suggested
                           that sleep was a new frontier in performance enhancement for athletes [27]. Sleep has a
                           restorative effect on the immune system and the endocrine system [28–30], facilitates the
                           recovery of the nervous and metabolic cost of the waking state and has an integral role
                           in cognitive function [31]. The relationship between sleep, nutrition and recovery is an
                           emerging area of interest [26,32–45]. Sleep has two basic states—non-rapid eye movement
                           sleep (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. NREM is subdivided into three
                           stages based on a continuum from light sleep (Stage N1 and N2) to deep sleep (Stage
                           N3). It has been hypothesised that sleep, especially slow-wave sleep (Stage N3), is vital
                           for physical recovery, due to the relationship with growth hormone release [44,46]. The
                           National Sleep Foundation has proposed 12 indicators of sleep quality including 4 sleep
                           continuity variables (sleep latency, awakenings >5 min, wake after sleep onset and sleep
                           efficiency), 5 sleep architecture variables (REM sleep, N1 sleep, N2 sleep, N3 sleep and
                           arousals) and 3 nap-related variables (naps per 24 h, nap duration and days per week
                           with at least one nap) [47]. Sleep can be considered adequate when there is no daytime
                           sleepiness or dysfunction.
                                  For sleep to have a restorative effect on the body, it must be of adequate duration,
                           quality, and appropriately timed [38,48]. The National Sleep Foundation has produced
                           guidelines regarding sleep duration for adolescents (recommended 8–10 h), adults (rec-
                           ommended 7–9 h), and older adults (7–8 h) [48]. It has been argued that elite athletes may
                           require more quality sleep than non-athletes [49]. It has recently been suggested that a one-
                           size-fits-all sleep recommendation (7–9 h) may be inappropriate for athlete performance
                           and health and an individual approach should be adapted including an assessment of
                           perceived sleep needs [50].
                                  Sleep inadequacy is common in athletes and can be attributed to the lack of an
                           appropriate sleep routine due to changing training schedules, timetables and other sleep-
 Nutrients 2021, 13, 1330                                                                                            3 of 25



                           incompatible behaviours, e.g., late night blue-light exposure [26,50]. Previous research has
                           reported sleep durations <7 h [51], long sleep onset latency [26,52], daytime sleepiness [53],
                           and daytime fatigue [54]. Studies investigating sleep quality in elite athletes have demon-
                           strated that 50–80% experience sleep disturbance and 22–26% experience highly disturbed
                           sleep [37,53,55]. Irregular sleep–wake patterns influence the homeostatic and circadian
                           regulation of sleep, which reduces both sleep quality and quantity [56]. For athletes, post-
                           completion routines and heightened arousal (i.e., medical care, recovery strategies, meals,
                           media commitments and travel) can lead to later bedtimes, which can adversely affect sleep
                           quality and quantity. Reduced sleep is associated with increased catabolic and reduced
                           anabolic hormones, which results in impaired muscle protein synthesis [12], potentially
                           blunting training adaptations and recovery.
                                 Sleep disorders are identified by a wide range of symptoms that impact health and
                           quality of life [57], cognitive performance [58] and physical performance [25,59]. Over
                           80 sleep disorders are listed in the third edition of the International Classification of Sleep
                           Disorders (ISCD-3) [60]. The ICSD-3 includes seven major categories of sleep disorders: in-
                           somnia, sleep-related breathing disorders, central disorders of hypersomnolence, circadian
                           rhythm sleep wake disorders (CRSWDs), sleep-related movement disorders, parasomnias
                           and other sleep disorders [60]. In the general population, the most common sleep disorders
                           are obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), insomnia and restless legs syndrome (RLS) [61]. Sleep-
                           related breathing disorders are characterised by breathing issues during sleep [62]. OSA is
                           a frequent condition characterised by repeated episodes of partial or complete reduction in
                           breathing activity during sleep [63]. Insomnia is characterised by difficulty falling asleep,
                           staying asleep, waking too early with daytime symptoms of fatigue, resistance to going to
                           bed and/or difficulty sleeping without intervention occurring at least 3 times per week
                           over a period of one month ([64,65]. Central disorders of hypersomnolence are typified by
                           excessive daytime sleepiness that cannot be attributed to another sleep disorder [60]. CR-
                           SWDs are chronic (≥3 months) patterns of sleep–wake disruption caused by an alteration to
                           the endogenous circadian or desychronisation of the circadian rhythm and the sleep–wake
                           schedule, causing sleep–wake disturbance and distress or impairment [60]. Sleep-related
                           movement disorders may result from an unpleasant crawling, deep-aching sensation in
                           the legs or arms that is relieved through movement [66]. Parasomnias are undesirable
                           movements or behaviours that occur during sleep, e.g., sleep walking, sleep talking, night
                           terrors and REM sleep behaviour disorder [66]. Other sleep disorders include all sleep
                           disorders that do not meet the criteria for another sleep disorder classifications [62].
                                 Polysomnography (PSG) is the ‘gold-standard’ method of sleep assessment and
                           records sleep continuity, sleep architecture and REM sleep. A common global approach to
                           the assessment of sleep quality is the use of self-report ratings reflecting an individual’s
                           satisfaction with their sleep [47,67]. Sleep continuity is commonly assessed using sleep
                           diaries and measures include time the subject went to bed, time the subject tried to initiate
                           sleep, the length of time from turning off the lights until sleep onset (sleep onset latency),
                           number and duration of awakenings, the degree of sleep maintenance during the night
                           (sleep efficiency or the ratio of wake time to time in bed; awake time after sleep onset) sleep
                           duration (total sleep time), time the subject woke up, time the subject got out of bed and
                           sleep quality (subjective rating of sleep) [68,69].
                                 Actigraphy is also used to assess sleep, regularly in combination with sleep diaries.
                           Actigraphy involves wearing a small monitor (usually on the non-dominant wrist) which
                           records body movement, high levels of activity are used as a measure of wakefulness and
                           low levels of activity are classified as sleep [69]. Activity monitors record movement as a
                           function of time [70], typically a tri-axial accelerometer is used to determine sleep/wake
                           based on a proprietary algorithm [71]. A limitation of actigraphy is that all activity is
                           recorded as waking unless the sleep diaries show an attempt to sleep (i.e., lying down trying
                           to sleep) and the activity counts are low enough to indicate the subject is stationary [32].
                           However, actigraphy has been shown to be reliable and valid in relation to PSG for general
                           measures of sleep [72,73].
 Nutrients 2021, 13, 1330                                                                                             4 of 25



                                  Athletes’ schedules can negatively impact their sleep and recovery [51,52], and the
                           repetitive demanding nature of a competitive season can also test athletes’ physiological
                           and psychological capacity, reinforcing the athletes’ need for quality sleep [74–77]. Actigra-
                           phy based sleep assessments reveal suboptimal sleep in athletes, i.e., low TST and high
                           WASO, causing resultant low sleep efficiency [27,30], which improves following a rest
                           day [78]. However, the athletes’ experience of suboptimal sleep remains unclear as sleep
                           need varies between individuals; some may report poor sleep while objective measures
                           indicate sufficient sleep [32]. Therefore, subjective measures of sleep quality, quantity and
                           timing are a valuable addition to objective sleep assessments. Combined subjective markers
                           of sleep (e.g., TST, time in bed, sleep efficiency, sleep quality and sleep onset latency) can
                           highlight the sleep need and recovery status of athletes and identify areas to be addressed
                           in terms of sleep optimisation. Moreover, the use of subjective measures within an athletic
                           population allows the assessment of large cohorts of athletes that are difficult to access, i.e.,
                           elite athletes.
                                  Animal models have demonstrated that nutrients such as glucose, amino acids,
                           sodium, ethanol and caffeine, as well as the timing of meals can affect circadian rhythms [79].
                           Neurotransmitters such as serotonin, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), orexin, dopamine,
                           melanin-concentrating hormone, galanin, noradrenaline and histamine that are involved
                           in the sleep–wake cycle [80] are affected by nutrition. In terms of recovery, the adaptive
                           response to training is dictated by a number of variables: duration, intensity, frequency
                           and type of exercise, in combination with timing, quality and quantity of nutrition both
                           pre- and post-exercise [81]. Recovery can be maximised by optimal nutrition practices or
                           reduced by suboptimal nutrition practices. Contemporary research has demonstrated the
                           pivotal role of both macronutrient and micronutrient availability in regulating skeletal
                           muscle adaptations to exercise [81–83]. It is important to characterise the sleep quality
                           and quantity of sub-elite and elite athletes and recovery practices. This study aimed to
                           investigate: (i) the quality, quantity and timing of sleep among sub-elite and elite athletes;
                           (ii) the recovery/stress balance of sub-elite and elite athletes; and (iii) the supplement use
                           and alcohol intake of sub-elite and elite athletes. This study also aimed to investigate the
                           difference between elite and sub-elite athletes in terms of their subjective sleep, recov-
                           ery and nutritional practices. It was hypothesised that the sleep, recovery and nutrition
                           practices of elite athletes would be superior to those of sub-elite athletes.

                           2. Materials and Methods
                           2.1. Participants
                                A sample (n = 338) comprising elite (n = 115; male n = 74 and female n = 41) and
                           sub-elite (n = 223; male 129 and female 94) athletes were recruited from both Ireland and
                           the United Kingdom (see Table 1). The elite athletes were recruited directly through Sport
                           Ireland and the national governing bodies (NGBs) of each sport within Ireland and the
                           United Kingdom. The sub-elite athletes were recruited via social media and the researcher’s
                           network within high-performance sport. In line with Swann et al. [84], elite athletes were
                           defined as: (a) currently receiving support/funding through the international carding
                           scheme and/or (b) members of a national/professional team or a recruitment/academy
                           squad and/or (c) nationally ranked in their sport. Sub-elite athletes were defined as those
                           competing at a regional, university and/or national level of organised sport that trained
                           and/or competed for a combined minimum of 400 min per week. Athletes, at either level,
                           were excluded if they were (i) aged <18 years, (ii) training and competing for <400 min per
                           week or (iii) reported a sleep disorder.

                            2.2. Procedure
                                 All eligible athletes were invited to take part in an online survey. All procedures
                            were approved by the research ethics committee of the Faculty of Health and Life Sciences,
                            Northumbria University (date of approval 2 July 2019; Submission ID: 17406). After
                            reading the participant information sheet, participants were invited to provide informed
                            consent and then completed an online survey on Qualtricsxm which consisted of a battery
                            of previously validated and reliable widely used questionnaires assessing sleep, recovery
                            and nutritional practices. Following completion of the survey, participants received a
                            debrief sheet with details of how they could contact the researcher if they wished to receive
                            feedback from the survey.

                            2.3. Measures
                                  In the initial section of the survey, the participants completed demographic data.
                            Participants recorded their gender, age, body mass (kg), height (cm), sport, athlete type
                            (elite or sub-elite), phase of season (pre-season, competition or off-season), normal training
                            time (before 8 a.m., 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and after 5 p.m.) and training/competition duration
                            per week (mins).

                            2.3.1. EuroQoL (EQ-5D-5L)
                                 The EQ-5D-5L is a self-report measure of health status as defined across five dimensions—
                            mobility, self-care, activity, pain and depression/anxiety—with one question per dimension.
                            Each dimension is scored on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = No problem to 5 = Severe prob-
                            lem) [85]. The EQ-5D-5L also includes a visual analogue scale on which respondents are
                            instructed to rate their perceived current health state (0–100). The EQ-5D-5L has capacity
                            to discriminate between slight, moderate and severe issues within each domain compared
                            to previous versions [86].

                            2.3.2. Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)
                                  The PSQI is a self-report measure of sleep quality [62]. The PSQI consists of 19 items
                            grouped into seven component scores (0–3) which are equally weighted. Although overall
                            global scores (GPSQI) are calculated by summing the seven components (range 0–21, with
                            higher scores indicating poorer sleep quality) the component scores provide subscale
                            ratings of: (i) subjective sleep quality, (ii) sleep latency, (iii) TST, (iv) sleep efficiency, (v)
                            sleep disturbances, (vi) use of sleep medication and (vii) daytime dysfunction [63]. Global
                            scores >5 are generally used to indicate poor sleep quality (63). The PSQI has demonstrated
                            a diagnostic sensitivity (89.6%) and specificity (86.5%) in distinguishing between ‘good’ and
                            poor’ sleepers [87]. However, more conservative scores of ≥8 have been used in athletes
                            to indicate poor sleep, potentially due to the increased sleep needs in this population [55].
                            Although the empirical discussion around the PSQI cut-offs for athletes is ongoing [38,55],
                            given that athletes often strive for marginal gains in their performance, which can be
                            facilitated through optimised sleep, the identification of both ‘poor’ and ‘moderate’ sleep
                            quality is warranted [43], hence the standard cut-off (≥5) was employed.
 Nutrients 2021, 13, 1330                                                                                            6 of 25



                           2.3.3. Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS)
                                The ESS is an eight-item self-report measure of general daytime sleepiness [88].
                           Respondents report their daytime sleepiness in particular situations on a Likert scale
                           (0 = Would never doze to 4 = High chance of dozing). Scores are summed to yield a global
                           ESS score (0–24). The EES global score is indicative of daytime sleepiness [89]. Higher
                           scores indicate greater sleepiness, scores >10 suggest excessive daytime sleepiness [88].
                           In general ESS scores are interpreted in terms of daytime sleepiness as follows: 0–5 low
                           normal, 6–10 higher normal, 11–12 mild excessive, 13–15 moderate excessive and 16–24
                           severe [65].

                           2.3.4. The Recovery Stress Questionnaire for Athletes (RESTQ Sport)
                                 The RESTQ-Sport is a 52-item self-report measure of general stress and recovery
                           levels of athletes [90]. The RESTQ-Sport consists of seven general stress components
                           with two items per scale (general stress, emotional stress, social stress, conflicts/pressure,
                           fatigue, a lack of energy, and physical complaints), five general recovery components
                           with two items per scale (success, social recovery, physical recovery, general well-being,
                           and sleep quality), three sport-specific stress components with four items per scale (dis-
                           turbed breaks, burnout/emotional exhaustion, and fitness/injury) and four sport-specific
                           recovery components with four items per scale (fitness/being in shape, burnout/personal
                           accomplishments, self-efficacy, and self-regulation) [90]. Sub-scale item mean scores can
                           be combined to give a total score for each of the four major sub-scales (i.e., general stress,
                           general recovery, sport-specific stress and sport-specific recovery). Each item is scored on
                           a Likert scale (0 = Never to 6 = Always) based on how often the respondent engaged in
                           a specified activity over the previous three days/nights, with a response of 0 indicating
                           never having experienced the feeling and 6 indicating always experiencing the associated
                           feeling. High scores on stress scales indicate a high level of stress, while high scores on the
                           recovery scales indicate a high level of recovery [90].

                           2.3.5. Athlete Morningness/Eveningness Questionnaire (AMES)
                                The AMES, which is based on the Horne–Östberg morningness/eveningness ques-
                           tionnaire [91], is a four-item questionnaire used to classify an athlete’s chronotype in terms
                           of self-identification as being a morning or evening type, preferred sleep/wake phase and
                           preferred competition and training time [92]. The AMES provides a global score which
                           is used to categorise chronotype: extreme evening type (10–12), moderate evening type
                           (13–17), mid-range type (18–23), moderate morning type (24–28) and extreme morning
                           type (29–31) [55].

                           2.3.6. Consensus Sleep Diary—Core (CSD-C)
                                 Participants were instructed to complete the CSD-C for two nights (1 ‘training/
                           competition’ day and 1 ‘rest’ day). The CSD is a standardised sleep diary developed
                           for use in both research and clinical settings [68]. The CSD-C included 8 items, e.g., bed
                           time, time it took to fall asleep, number of awakenings, duration of awakenings, time of
                           final awakening, time the respondent got out of bed, and a Likert scale self-report rating
                           of sleep quality [93]. There was also a comments section where participants could record
                           specific comments about each night’s sleep (i.e., 1 training/competition day and 1 rest day).
                           The data collected were then used to compute indices of sleep continuity such as total time
                           in bed (TIB), total sleep time (TST, sleep onset latency (SOL; time from lights out to N1),
                           wakefulness after sleep onset (WASO; amount of time awake after sleep onset), number of
                           awakenings (NoA) and sleep efficiency (SE; ratio of TST:TIB) [93].

                           2.4. Supplementation
                               All participants were instructed to complete questions relating to supplement use
                           (name, dose, frequency and reason for use) on both training/competition days and rest
 Nutrients 2021, 13, 1330                                                                                               7 of 25



                           days. Athletes also reported their alcohol consumption (number of drinking sessions and
                           unit consumption per session) in the last month prior to completion of the questionnaire.

                           2.5. Data Analysis
                                All data were analysed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS
                           Version 25, IBM Corporation) and Jamovi (Version 1.8.16). Frequency distribution and
                           descriptive statistics were used to present findings [94]. All data were presented as the mean
                           ± standard deviation, and/or frequency. The differences between the groups for athlete
                           type were explored using independent-samples t-tests, chi square tests, Mann–Whitney U
                           and one-way ANOVA [94].

                           3. Results
                           3.1. Participant Characteristics
                                A total of 338 (elite n = 115 and sub-elite n = 223) athletes were recruited from a variety
                           of team and individual sports (see Tables 1 and 2.). The sample consisted of both male
                           (n = 203; ~60%) and female (n = 135; ~40%) athletes.

                                 A chi square analysis demonstrated no significant differences between the groups for
                           gender (X2 [1, n = 338] = 1.72, p = 0.189). While there were statistically significant differ-
                           ences between the groups for age (elite 23.44 ± 4.91 years and sub-elite 25.71 ± 6.27 years;
                           t(336) = 3.38; p = 0.001) and minutes trained per week (elite 801.35 ± 338.81 and sub-elite
                           610.02 ± 266.90; t(336) = −5.68; p ≤ 0.001). An independent-samples t-test indicated no
                           significant differences between the groups in terms of height, body mass and normal
                           training time (time of day when training occurred) (see Table 1).
                                 Chi square analyses demonstrated a statistically significant difference between the
                           groups for sport (X2 [9, n = 338] = 1.72, p ≤ 0.001). There were no statistically significant
                           differences between the groups for phase of season: pre-season (elite n = 31; sub-elite
                           n = 57), competition (elite n = 65; sub-elite n = 115), off-season (elite n = 19; sub-elite n = 51)
                           (X2 [2, n = 338] = 1.88, p = 0.39). There were statistically significant differences between the
                           groups for normal training time: before 8 am (elite n = 8 and sub-elite n = 25), between
                           8 a.m. and 5 p.m. (elite n = 50; sub-elite n = 58), and after 5 p.m. (elite n = 57; sub-elite
                           n = 140) (X2 [2, n = 338] = 10.9, p ≤ 0.001).

                           3.1.1. EuroQoL
                                 There was no statistically significant difference between the groups for their perceived
                           general health rating (0–100) with the elite athlete group reporting slightly higher levels of
                           general health than the sub-elite athlete group (83.05 ± 13.65 vs. 81.05 ± 12.57; t = −1.37;
                           p = 0.172). There were no statistically significant differences between the groups in terms
                           of each of the domains of the quality of life measure (see Table 3). Slight to severe problems
                           with mobility were reported by 19% (n = 65) of participants (elite n = 19 [17%]; sub-
                           elite n = 46 [21%]). Some issues regarding the completion of usual activities (e.g., work,

                           of participants (elite n = 23 [20%]; sub-elite n = 41 [18%]). Issues with self-care were not
                           evident within the athletes as slight to moderate issues were reported by 3% of participants
                           (elite n = 2 [2%]; sub-elite n = 9 [4%]). Pain was reported by 50% (n = 169) of participants
                           (elite n = 53 [46%]; sub-elite n = 116 [52%]). Anxiety/depression was reported by 34%
                           (n = 116) of participants (elite n = 43 [37%]; sub-elite n = 73 [33%]).

                           3.1.2. Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index
                                 An independent-samples t-test was used to compare PSQI data for the elite and sub-
                           elite athlete groups. A statistically significant difference was observed between the groups
                           for PSQI habitual sleep efficiency % (elite 88.62 ± 8.84 vs. sub-elite 86.55 ± 9.09; t = −2.01;
                           p = 0.046). While no other statistically significant differences were observed, the majority
                           of athletes (64%; n = 220) were classified as poor sleepers (i.e., global PSQI score ≥5—elite

                           as the athletes rated their sleep quality as very good (elite n = 19 [17%]; sub-elite n = 45
                           [20%]), fairly good (elite n = 68 [59%]; sub-elite n = 123 [55%]), fairly bad (elite n = 26 [23%];
                           sub-elite n = 50 [22%]) and poor (elite n = 2 [1%]; sub-elite n = 5 [2%]). Mean total sleep time
                           (hours) varied between the elite athlete (7.58 ± 1.06; range 5–10 h) and the sub-elite athlete
                           groups (7.35 ± 1.05; range 4–10 h) but this was not statistically significant. The athletes
                           reported total sleep time ≤6 h (elite n = 16 [14%]; sub-elite n = 43 [19%]), 7 h (elite n = 38
                           [33%]; sub-elite n = 80 [36%]), 8 h (elite n = 39 [34%]; sub-elite n = 70 [32%]) and 9 h (elite
                           n = 22 [19%]; sub-elite n = 30 [13%]). The athletes’ responses to the PSQI are summarised
                           in Table 3. The athletes reported total time in bed 8 h (elite n = 53 [46%]; sub-elite n = 109
                           [49%]), 9–10 h (elite n = 50 [44%]; sub-elite n = 110 [49%]) and 11–12 h (elite n = 12 [10%];
                           sub-elite n = 4 [2%]).

                           waking during the night or early morning, waking to use the bathroom and feeling too hot

                           week was reported by 44% (n = 51) of the elite group and 41% (n = 92) of the sub-elite group.

769	                                4. Discussion
770	                                      This study recruited a large cohort of elite (n = 115) and sub-elite (n = 223) athletes
771	                                from a wide variety of sports. Elite athletes were either international athletes, members of
772	                                a national/professional team, a recruitment/academy squad and/or nationally ranked in
773	                                their sport [84]. Sub-elite athletes were defined as those competing at a regional, university
774	                                and/or national level of organised sport that trained and/or competed for a combined
775	                                minimum of 400 min per week [84]. To the authors’ knowledge, this is one of the largest
776	                                cohorts of athletes to have been investigated from a sleep and recovery perspective. This
777	                                study aimed to investigate: the quality, quantity and timing of sleep among sub-elite and
778	                                elite athletes and characterise their recovery and nutrition practices. It was hypothesised
779	                                that the sleep, recovery and nutrition practices of elite athletes would be superior to those of
780	                                sub-elite athletes. Interestingly, similar levels of poor sleep were reported by both the elite
781	                                and sub-elite athlete groups, whereas there was a significant difference in sport-specific
782	                                recovery practices.
783

786	                                diaries that athletes reported improved TIB, TST and WASO on rest days. Excessive daytime
787	                                sleepiness was also observed in both groups. Similarly, previous research has suggested

793	                           potentially inadequate in relation to optimal recovery and performance [27,30,32,37,95].

795	                           4.2. Pittsburg Sleep Quality Index
796	                                The PSQI has demonstrated good reliability (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.83, test–retest
797	                           reliability r = 0.85) [87]. The PSQI having demonstrated acceptable internal consistency
798	                           and has been shown to be reliable [96,97] and valid [87,96–98] measure of sleep quality.
799	                           Cronbach’s alpha 0.744 was observed in the current sample. The majority of athletes (~65%;
800	                           n = 220) were classified as poor sleepers (Global PSQI score ≥5). This is consistent with pre-
801	                           vious research in elite athletes [53–55,95], and sub-elite athletes [99,100]. A relatively high
802	                           proportion of athletes (~30%) self-reported their sleep quality as either poor or very poor
803	                           on the training/competition day compared to rest day (elite 10% [n = 12] and sub-elite 16%
804	                           [n = 36]). The PSQI data highlighted reasons for poor sleep on both training/competition
805	                           days and rest days such as feeling too hot in bed and a lack of enthusiasm for general tasks.
806	                           Poor sleep quality is of particular concern for elite athletes as it can result in a reduction in
807	                           recovery and/or subsequent athletic performance [29,101–103].
808	                                Interestingly the PSQI mean TST (<8 h) was lower than that reported in the CSD-C
809	                           (>8 h), it has been suggested that athletes tend to overestimate their sleep [104,105]. A
810	                           recent review suggested that sleep in athletes is limited to 7.2 h per night, with all studies
811	                           reporting <8 h per night and mean SE was 86.3 ± 6.8% [106], which is in line with the PSQI
812	                           and CSD-C data from the current study. The PSQI mean TST for both groups in the current
813	                           study is adequate according to current sleep recommendations (7–9 h) [48]. However,
814	                           optimal TST is subject to individual variance and it has been argued that elite athletes may
815	                           require more quality sleep than non-athletes [49]. It has previously been reported that
816	                           athletes tend to sleep less (6.5–6.7 h) and that their sleep quality is poor [27,54,107–109].
817	                           Optimising sleep gives athletes an advantage when it comes to maximising adaptations
818	                           from training and performance enhancement [110].

823	                           days. However, it did improve on the rest day which was most likely a reflection of their
824	                           behaviour, e.g., choosing to go to bed earlier. Although not statistically significant there was
825	                           a trend towards reduced TIB, TST and WASO in both groups on the rest day while the elite

855	                           4.3.1. Daytime Sleepiness
856	                                 The ESS score is comparable to objective sleepiness measures such as the multiple
857	                           sleep latency test (MSLT) and is considered a valid and reliable measure of objective sleepi-
858	                           ness [88]. The ESS has been widely used in athletic populations such as Australian rules
859	                           football [116], collegiate basketball players [109] and American football players [117]. In the
860	                           present sample, Cronbach’s alpha was 0.827. Approximately 21% of athletes in the current
861	                           study reported excessive daytime sleepiness. Similar levels of excessive daytime sleepiness
862	                           have been reported in rugby players and cricketers [53], American footballers [117], Aus-
863	                           tralian rules footballers [116] and college athletes [99]. Similarly, previous research reported
864	                           that 44% (n = 12) Brazilian Paralympians experienced excessive daytime sleepiness [118].
865	                           However, it must be noted that these athletes may have had physical impairments (e.g.,
866	                           spinal cord injury) that could impact sleep quantity and quality.
867	                                 The levels of excessive daytime sleepiness observed in the current study may be due
868	                           to sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and periodic limb movement
869	                           disorder (PLMD). In the general population, the most common sleep disorders are (OSA),
870	                           insomnia and restless legs syndrome (RLS)/(PLMD) [61]. OSA is a frequent condition
871	                           characterised by repeated episodes of partial or complete reduction in breathing activity
872	                           during sleep [61]. PLMD is a condition characterised by repetitive limb movements
873	                           during sleep that cause sleep disruption [62]. A recent systematic review highlighted
874	                           the prevalence of insomnia symptoms (longer SOL, increased sleep fragmentation and
875	                           excessive daytime sleepiness) in elite athletes [37]. Other sleep problems such as OSA are
876	                           less prevalent but appear to higher in strength and power athletes (e.g., rugby players) most
877	                           likely due to increased body mass and neck circumference (>42 cm) which are anatomical
878	                           features related to OSA [53]. A recent study using a combination of PSG and subjective
879	                           measures demonstrated a high prevalence of sleep disorders in Rugby union players
880	                           (n = 25), all players displayed insomnia symptoms and 24% (n = 6) had OSA and 12%
881	                           (n = 3) [64]. In similar study using home-based PSG in rugby league players (n = 22), 45%
882	                           (n = 10) had OSA [119]. A previous study of NFL players (n = 137) demonstrated that
883	                           19% (n = 26) had OSA [120]. Previous research in elite ice hockey players (n = 107) has
884	                           demonstrated sleep problem, 11% (n = 14) had insomnia, 10% (n = 13) had OSA and 3%
885	                           (n = 4) had RLS/PLMD [26]. Athletes with poor sleep habits and/or a sleep disorder must
886	                           be identified and diagnosed and individual interventions (e.g., sleep hygiene, nutrition)
887	                           must be implemented in order to athlete recovery and performance.

895	                           majority of the athletes from both groups 58% (n = 197) indicated that their normal training

897	                           A study investigating the sleep quality of morning and evening types after a morning

901	                           morning session was similar for both groups [121]. The late training times reported by the

912	                           4.4. Recovery
913	                                Recovery is a process in time, dependent on the duration of stress and requires a
914	                           reduction in stress, a change in stress or a break from stress [123,124]. Relatively high levels
915	                           of fatigue, stress and pain were reported in both groups. A range of supplements were
916	                           used regularly by athletes in both groups; indeed, whey was the most commonly used
917	                           recovery supplement in both groups. The results suggest that future research is warranted
918	                           to further the development of individualised inventions focused on sleep, nutrition and
919	                           athlete recovery.

921	                           4.4.1. EuroQoL
922	                                 The EQ-5D-5L has demonstrated reliability (mean intraclass correlation coefficients
923	                           0.69; range 0.43–0.84) and convergent validity (mean Spearman rank coefficients 0.99; range
924	                           0.97–0.99) [85]. Cronbach’s alpha of 0.70–0.95 are considered “acceptable” for a scale used
925	                           in human research [125,126]. Cronbach’s alpha 0.609 was observed in the current sample
926	                           most likely due to the low number of items (5), as the size if alpha depends on the number
927	                           of items in a scale [127]. The mean general health rating scores for the elite athlete group
928	                           (83.1 ± 12.6) and the sub-elite athlete group (81 ± 13.7) were relatively high, which was
929	                           consistent with current research in athletes [128]. In the current study, the elite athlete
930	                           group reported higher mean health rating scores. Elite athletes tend to have their training
931	                           and recovery sessions scheduled for them [54], hence, they are likely to complete regular
932	                           if not daily mobility type sessions. Whereas the sub-elite athletes may have had less free
933	                           time due to work, social and family commitments. A high prevalence of pain was reported
934	                           by 50% (n = 169) of participants (elite n = 53 sub-elite n = 116). An investigation of ‘mildly
935	                           sleepy’ (indicative of inadequate TST) but otherwise healthy males (n = 24) showed sleep
936	                           extension (time in bed 10 h) increased pain tolerance by 20% [129]. While chronic sleep
937	                           restriction (50% of habitual time for 12 days) is related to increased levels of muscle soreness
938	                           and increased pain sensitivity [107]. While mobility issues were noted in both groups, there
939	                           were higher levels mobility issues reported by the sub-elite athlete group coupled with
940	                           issues completing usual activities. However, it has recently been suggested that elite and
941	                           high-level athletes have increased pain tolerance (cold pressor test) and that the training
942	                           time per week has a positive impact on the tolerance [130].

944	                           4.4.2. REST-Q Sport
945	                                 The RESTQ-Sport has been shown to be valid in athletic populations [131,132]. The
946	                           scales have displayed good internal consistency (0.67–0.89) and high test–retest reliability
947	                           (>0.79) [90,124]. A Cronbach’s alpha of 0.784 was observed in the current sample.
948	                                 Relatively high levels of stress and fatigue were evident from the REST-Q. Stress and
949	                           fatigue are factors for illness, which must be managed by elite athletes [133,134], during
950	                           their competitive seasons to avoid missed training/competitions. Significant differences
951	                           between the elite and sub-elite athletes were observed for four of the REST-Q subscales
952	                           relating to athletic performance, with higher mean score for each subscale: being in shape,
953	                           personal accomplishment, self-efficacy and self-regulation reported by the elite athlete
954	                           group. The injury (2.31 ± 1.17 vs. 2.48 ± 1.09), fatigue (2.45 ± 1.32 vs. 2.54 ± 1.32) subscale
955	                           scores were relatively high in both the elite athletes and sub-elite athletes, while the sleep
956	                           quality scores were low (2.76 ± 0.78 vs. 2.83 ± 0.85). The current findings are consistent
957	                           with previous research which reported that injury risk was significantly positively related
958	                           to injury subscale scores for disturbed breaks, fatigue, and lower values on the sleep quality
959	                           subscale score [131]. The relationship between training load and health can be considered
960	                           on a well-being continuum [123,134,135], with training load and recovery as antagonists.
961	                           Stress is imposed on athletes, altering their physical and psychological well-being along a

975	                           2.91 ± 0.90) were reported by the elite athlete group compared to the sub-elite athlete group.
976	                           This result potentially highlights the fact that elite athletes tend to be under the supervision
977	                           of a multidisciplinary team, e.g., medical, strength and conditioning, nutrition, physiology
978	                           and psychology, who are involved in all aspects of the athletes training and recovery.
979	                           The sub-elite athletes would typically not receive the same access to multidisciplinary
980	                           support services. It is imperative that athletes have a detailed recovery plan compromising
981	                           of nutrition, hydration, sleep and psychological recovery [134]. Given the high training
982	                           and competition load that athletes undertake, it is clear that they must adopt strategies
983	                           that promote sleep across the domains of quality, quantity and timing. Fatigue can be
984	                           managed, and recovery enhanced through adequate passive rest and sufficient sleep [137],
985	                           it is generally recommended that athletes have at least one ‘rest’ day per week. Rest
986	                           days can serve to alleviate boredom and stress perception while the absence of a ‘rest
987	                           day’ during periods of intense training has been related to the onset overreaching and
988	                           inadequate recovery [137]. It is suggested from the current results that sleep tends to
989	                           improve on rest days, i.e., increased perceived sleep quality, TIB, TST and reduced WASO
990	                           in both groups, while SL, NOA and SE also improved in the elite athlete group.

992	                           4.5. Nutrition
993	                                In the current sample, the elite athletes tended to consume more supplements, at
994	                           higher doses with increased frequency, compared to the sub-elite athletes. Those athletes
995	                           who used supplements reported high usage of caffeine, whey protein, creatine, multivita-
996	                           mins, fish oil, probiotics and vitamin D while the use of iron and nitrate was reported to a
997	                           lesser extent. This is similar to previous research in elite Dutch athletes (n = 778) where the
998	                           most commonly consumed supplements were multivitamins, caffeine, vitamin D, sports
999	                           drinks, protein, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate [138]. It has also been demonstrated
1000	                           previously that elite athletes tend to take more supplements than sub-elite athletes [139].
1001	                           Despite the relatively low number of athletes reporting supplement use, the correlations
1002	                           between supplement use and RESTQ scales warrant further investigation. Whey protein
1003	                           was one of the most prevalent supplements used while casein use was also reported. While
1004	                           research is emerging supporting pre-sleep protein ingestion for muscle recovery [140,141],
1005	                           the impact of pre-sleep ingestion of 40 g doses of whey and/or casein warrants further
1006	                           investigation with regards both muscle recovery and sleep improvement.
1007	                                Daily caffeine use was reported by approximately 20% of the athletes which could neg-
1008	                           atively impact sleep. The low level of caffeine use reported in the current study was most
1009	                           likely due to the fact that athletes were asked to report their supplement use and may have
1010	                           neglected to include habitual caffeine consumption. Caffeine exerts a stimulant effect pro-
1011	                           moting alertness by blocking adenosine receptors [142]. The levels of caffeine consumption
1012	                           reported were lower than previous research which has suggested that 75–90% of athletes
1013	                           consume caffeine before or during competition [143–145]. While, it has been suggested that
1014	                           chronic low dose caffeine ingestion may blunt any potential ergogenic effects [146], moder-
1015	                           ate doses (~3 mg/kg/d) appear to pose no problems for most athletes [147]. However, in
1016	                           terms of sleep, moderate caffeine doses have been shown to increase SOL and decrease TST,
1017	                           REM sleep and SE [148]. Hence, athletes training/competing in the late afternoon (>5 p.m.)
1018	                           need to consider its potentially detrimental effect on sleep. It has recently been suggested
1019	                           that athletes should adopt a strategic individualised approach to caffeine consumption

1034	                           4.6. Limitations
1035	                                 Due to logistical reasons, the sleep diary was only completed for one training/
1036	                           competition day and one rest day, and this may have been insufficient in terms of data
1037	                           collection. It has been recommended that sleep diaries should be completed for a duration
1038	                           of 1 week [68,153]. The aim of the 2 day diary was to limit participant burden and recall
1039	                           bias [154]. However, sleep diaries may be more accurate than sleep questionnaires [32].
1040	                           The intrinsic limitations of self-report measures (i.e., questionnaires and diaries) are mea-
1041	                           surement error and recall bias [94]. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that athletes can
1042	                           overestimate their TST [104,105]. However, self-report measures have their place within ath-
1043	                           letic settings, as they are a relatively simple and inexpensive approach to athlete monitoring
1044	                           affording a more representative overview of the target population [44]. Within elite athlete
1045	                           populations, the use of subjective measures of sleep are often employed, particularly during
1046	                           the competitive season due to the more invasive nature of both PSG and actigraphy [12]. A
1047	                           growing body of research has suggested that self-report measures may be more sensitive
1048	                           and reliable than physiological, biochemical and performance measures [44,137,153–156].
1049	                           When choosing a particular measure, ultimately the aim is to maintain a balance between
1050	                           the need to obtain meaningful data from an athlete whilst minimising the burden involved
1051	                           in completion of any self-report measure [154–156]. In the current study, it was not fea-
1052	                           sible or practical due to the large sample size to include a subjective assessment of sleep.
1053	                           However, future research should incorporate both objective (e.g., PSG, actigraphy) and
1054	                           subjective measures (e.g., sleep diaries) of sleep to provide a more accurate estimates of
1055	                           sleep and because some individuals may self-report poor sleep quality despite objective
1056	                           measures indicating adequate sleep [155–157]. There was little difference between the elite
1057	                           and sub-elite athlete groups in terms of sleep. The inclusion of a healthy control group
1058	                           would have allowed for comparison and exploration of the differences between the sleep
1059	                           of athletic population and healthy adults.
1060	                                 A specific section in relation to anxiety/depression could have been included in
1061	                           the battery of questionnaires given the potential to impact on sleep and vice versa. The
1062	                           Profile of Mood States (POMS) [158] is widely used in wellness assessments of athletic
1063	                           populations and has subscales that specifically relate to anxiety and depression. However,
1064	                           as the EuroQoL has a dimension for anxiety/depression, the POMS was omitted to reduce
1065	                           participant burden and survey fatigue which could have negatively impacted the reliability
1066	                           of the data collected.
1067	                                 The demographic difference between the groups was a limitation in that there was
1068	                           a statistically significant difference between the groups with the sub-elite group being
1069	                           significantly older which could have affected the results. This issue was directly related to
1070	                           the sampling method employed where participants are recruited based on their accessibility.
1071	                           However, care was taken to recruit a large cohort (n = 338) and strict inclusion and exclusion
1072	                           criteria were applied [84].

1076	                           of large cohorts of athletes. Such studies should include a combination of subjective and
1077	                           objective measures of sleep and recovery, for a minimum of 1 week [54,153]. The validity

1085	                                  As the majority of athletes in the current cohort have reported sleep problems future
1086	                           research is warranted to identify the specific sleep problems that affect athletic populations.
1087	                           It is also necessary in future research to identify if athletes are affected by acute disturbances,
1088	                           e.g., competition anxiety or chronic disorders, e.g., OSA, insomnia and PLMD [26].
1089	                                  Future research should investigate the effects of specific nutritional recovery strategies
1090	                           (e.g., antioxidants, protein, carbohydrate) on sleep in athletic populations. Such practices
1091	                           may already be an established part of an athlete’s daily routine, but the potential additional
1092	                           benefit of improved sleep must be explored.

1094	                           4.8. Practical Applications
1095	                                 A strength of this novel study is that it presents ‘real-life’ data from training/competition
1096	                           days and a rest day relating to the sleep and recovery practices of athletes. Poor sleep and
1097	                           inadequate recovery practices were evident in both the elite and sub-elite athlete groups.
1098	                           In a recent study, 95% of swimmers (n = 82) identified their coaches (n = 10) as the primary
1099	                           source of recovery information while the coaches highlighted conferences and workshops
1100	                           as their primary source of recovery information [159]. In order to promote sleep hygiene
1101	                           and adequate recovery practices in athletes, a comprehensive coach and athlete education
1102	                           curriculum may need to be developed and implemented.
1103	                                 The athletes generally reported improved sleep quality and quantity on rest days
1104	                           which has implications for athlete health, well-being and performance. Optimising the
1105	                           sleep and recovery practices of athletes would impact performance. Monitoring of sleep
1106	                           behaviours, nutrition and recovery-stress responses of athletes aids the identification of
1107	                           irregularities (e.g., due to travel or illness) and allows for early interventions with individual
1108	                           athletes as and when necessary [157]. The ongoing collection of data from athletes such as
1109	                           the data collected in the current study could be used by coaches and medical and support
1110	                           staff to implement individual sleep, recovery and nutrition interventions and plans.

1112	                           5. Conclusions
1113	                                 Due to the symbiosis between sleep and recovery, it is clear from the current findings
1114	                           that athletes should have a detailed individualised and multifaceted recovery plan in place
1115	                           involving sleep, nutrition, hydration, and other physiological and psychological aspects.
1116	                           At the elite level, athletes and their support teams continually strive for marginal gains
1117	                           over time to improve performance (135). Training and competition load elicit a number of
1118	                           homeostatic responses and adaptations, and the main aim of training is to exploit these in
1119	                           order to elicit an improvement in performance. The training process involves exploitation,
1120	                           manipulation and coordination of numerous variables (e.g., physiology, biomechanics and
1121	                           psychology) to improve performance. Athletes continually strive to improve their perfor-
1122	                           mance, and, as such, variations in training load are necessary, e.g., increased frequency,
1123	                           duration and/or intensity in order to optimise the training response [44]. Depending on

1125	                           must be managed to increase or decrease fatigue, to enhance training adaptations or per-
